🗒️What This Means For You
  • Stocks: US stocks ended flat; Europe fell about half a percent; Japan rose.
  • FX: Dollar edged up; euro, pound, yen and yuan barely moved today.
  • Technicals: Stocks and yields sit well above their averages; stretched, trend still intact.
  • Sectors: Tech and media lead; rate-sensitive utilities, property and materials keep sinking.
  • Credit/Spreads: Companies still borrow very cheaply; lenders demand almost no extra reward.
  • Crisis: Main risks: government debt and oil shocks. Banks and credit look calm.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is cooling slowly, but more than half of prices still run hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip stocks and credit look like 2000; the overall market doesn't yet.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron reports Sept 30 with huge expectations; Jabil options price a big move.
  • Iran: Iran offered a 60-day truce plan and gave the US days to reply.
  • Warsh: Fed raised rates in September; Warsh's Fed leans toward more hikes.
  • Week Ahead: Next week: PCE inflation, job openings, Micron and Nike results, Iran deadline.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral; rising yields and oil lean us cautious over months.
  • Trades: Cut junk-bond risk, bet on steeper curve, own energy, skip Micron gamble.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 24 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.99 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 100th pctile, +0bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Bonds and oil are sending warnings; stocks and credit are ignoring them.

The day's story came from bonds and oil, not stocks. The US 10Y rose 8.36bp to 5.1978% and the 30Y rose 7.71bp to 5.476%. Yields also rose abroad: JGB 10Y +9.1bp to 3.08%, Bund +4.4bp to 3.599%, Gilt +3.4bp to 5.381%. Brent jumped 3.66% to 106.85 and WTI rose 2.66% to 94.61. Iran has put a clock on its UN ceasefire road map, giving Washington 'four to five days' (globalsecurity.org, Day 209, 24-Sep). US stocks barely moved versus the prior session: S&P 500 -0.02% at 7704.13, Nasdaq +0.01%, Dow -0.31%, Russell 2000 -0.11%. Europe was weaker: STOXX 600 -0.55%, Euro Stoxx 50 -0.43%. The Nikkei gained 0.76%. The VIX rose 0.49 to 15.67, which is still a calm reading. Sentiment is complacent-to-neutral. Credit spreads sit near the tightest levels in their history (IG 2nd percentile, EM 2nd, HY 7th; computed). Retail sentiment is actually bearish (AAII bull-bear -15.4). The disconnect is clear: rates and energy are pricing risk, while equity and credit risk premia are not.

“The bond market is shouting and stocks aren't listening. When rates and oil both climb, someone has to blink, and it's rarely the bond market.”

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Growth leads and rate-sensitive defensives are being hit. US 1-month: Info Tech +6.64%, Comm Services +4.7% and Energy +1.32% are the only gainers. Utilities -8.71%, Real Estate -7.36%, Materials -6.99%, Financials -6.25%, Cons Discr -5.28% and Industrials -5.2% all fell. YTD, Energy (+36.76%) and Info Tech (+27.02%) dominate, while Utilities (-8.86%) and Cons Discr (-3.92%) trail. Today Comm Services (+1.92%), Health Care (+0.65%) and Energy (+0.43%) led, while Utilities (-1.02%), Materials (-1.01%) and Staples (-0.97%) lagged. The global picture matches: Info Tech +5.86% 1m and +34.46% YTD, Utilities -6.68% 1m, Materials -7.75% 1m. This is not a classic cyclical-vs-defensive rotation. Bond-proxy defensives are losing to 5%+ yields, economically sensitive cyclicals are losing to the oil and rate squeeze, and only mega-cap growth and energy are holding up. The market is narrowing. Financials' -6.25% 1m slide despite a steeper curve deserves attention (analyst view).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.99 vol points (81th percentile of the 26 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 104.6 (76th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 101bp (steeper by 40bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Right rim5.20%2026-09-24

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (96bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.20 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed path chart anchors the current cycle at Oct-2022, now at month 47 with an index of 245.2. On the Oct-1990 anchor, the dot-com run was at 231.7 in month 47 and did not peak until month 113 (1423.9). On the Jun-1994 reset anchor, it peaked in month 69. Price action alone therefore places us closer to the mid-1990s than to the 2000 top. Valuation is the biggest gap: the Nasdaq trailing P/E is 38.73x against 175x at the peak (computed marker 22%). The 2000-style tell is in semis, which are near peak-mania multiples. Tight credit, low VIX and loose financial conditions also exceed 2000 levels. What differs from 1999–2000 is that yields are rising fast (10Y at 5.1978%) with a positive, steepening curve. The more likely risk is a rate-driven de-rating of long-duration growth rather than a classic inverted-curve recession bust. The drawdown benchmark: the Nasdaq fell 78.0% from 5048.62 (2000-03-10) to 1114.11 (2002-10-09) over 31 months. The analyst-estimate inputs (concentration ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~210%, IPO froth 30, LT EPS-growth expectations 70) were NOT verified by web search this run because the search budget was used on required news topics. Treat them as approximate.

⚔️Iran War

Day 209 of the war, which the US and Israel began on Feb 28, 2026. At the UN, Iran gave the US a road map for a region-wide ceasefire of up to 60 days, a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to the American blockade. It also includes a halt to Iranian attacks on Arab neighbours and a timeline for substantive talks during the truce. Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Washington has four to five days to accept Iran's seven conditions. Iran has not withdrawn its demand that the Saudi blockade of Houthi-held areas be lifted (GlobalSecurity, 24-Sep). Al Jazeera's 23-Sep live blog reports Trump confirming a 'very good meeting' with Iran at the UN, and Tehran saying it is ready for 'dialogue, diplomacy without force'. Pressure is also escalating. A Treasury aviation-denial measure took effect Sept 23, cutting Iranian carriers off from fuel, landing services and ticketing worldwide, and the UAE suspended Iranian carrier flights. Khaleej Times reports the US Senate rejected a resolution to curb Trump's Iran war powers. Market read (analyst view): diplomacy and escalation are running side by side, and Brent's +3.66% to 106.85 shows oil still pricing supply risk. The 4–5 day deadline makes early next week a binary for energy.

Sources: Iran War 2026 -- Day 209 Update -- 24 September 2026 (GlobalSecurity) · Iran war updates: Tehran ready for 'dialogue, diplomacy without force' (Al Jazeera, 23-Sep) · US senate rejects resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers (Khaleej Times, 24-Sep) · 2026 Iran war (Britannica)

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting (inferred): hold, with a hiking bias. The Fed raised rates 25bp to 3.75–4.00% on Sept 16. Warsh has said there is 'work to do' on inflation, and his Jackson Hole speech was read as hawkish. With Core PCE at 3.34415 and Brent above $100, analyst estimate ~40% odds of a back-to-back 25bp hike and ~60% hold-and-signal. This is inference, not guidance.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from on-record statements: policy rate 4.00–4.50% within ~12 months (analyst estimate). The fed funds rate stays the main policy tool, while the balance sheet is steadily shortened in duration through the Balance Sheet Task Force he created in June 2026. That likely adds to term premium and a steeper curve. Cuts are unlikely unless the oil shock turns into a growth shock.

Warsh's record is consistently hawkish on inflation credibility and skeptical of a large Fed balance sheet. He held rates in July while promising to 'deliver price stability', gave a Jackson Hole speech that analysts said raised hike odds and could put the Fed 'at odds' with Treasury, and then hiked in September. BlackRock/iShares notes that his emphasis on short-term rates as the main policy tool implies continued shortening of the balance sheet's duration. My inference: with the 10Y already at 5.1978% and the 2s10s at +27.35bp, a Warsh Fed will tolerate a steeper curve and higher long-end yields rather than lean against them. Estimates here are flagged as inference.

Sources: September 16, 2026 Chairman Warsh's Press Conference (Federal Reserve) · Jackson Hole analyst roundup: Warsh's speech sends hike chances higher (CNBC, 31-Aug) · Kevin Warsh Says There's Still 'Work to Do' to Fight Inflation (Chase) · Fed Outlook 2026: Rate forecasts and fixed income strategies (iShares)
